*This synod is convinced that the forces of the Allies are being used of God to vindicate the rights of the weak and to maintain the moral order of the world.*
— Anglican Synod, Melbourne, 1916

It was strange at first—
That wide, staring look in his eyes,
The hair falling past his shoulders—
But after a visit to the ship's barber,
A saltwater shower, and the old slouch hat
Pulled low across his ears,
He began to look the part.

It took him some time to master
How a bayonet fits the old Lee-Enfield,
But going in on the boats,
He seemed calmer than any of us,
Simply gazing out over the swell
Where the cliffs stood black against the sky.

When we struck the shore, he tore through the waves,
Then up the beach, weaving like a full-back
As the Turks bore down hard upon us.
By the time the rest of us caught up,
He was already gone—flashing up the cliffs
Toward the first machine gun.

He'd accounted for three Turks by the time we arrived;
The fourth was left a quivering wreck.
Watching him raise that blood-stained bayonet,
I knew then we were glad
To have him fighting on our side.

# The Making of a Soldier: Faith, Transformation, and Valor in Wartime Australia

## The Church's Endorsement of the War Effort

In 1916, the Anglican Synod convened in Melbourne and issued a striking declaration that would echo the sentiments of many religious institutions during the First World War. The Synod expressed its firm conviction that the Allied forces were not merely fighting for political or territorial gain, but were serving as instruments of divine will. According to this declaration, God himself was employing the Allied armies to defend the weak and vulnerable nations of the world, while simultaneously upholding the moral and ethical order that was perceived to be under threat from the aggressive actions of the Central Powers. This theological framing of the war provided spiritual justification for the sacrifices being demanded of young Australian men, transforming military service into a form of righteous crusade blessed by divine sanction.

## An Unlikely Recruit

Against this backdrop of religious fervor and patriotic duty, the poem in question introduces us to a soldier who initially cut a peculiar figure among his fellow servicemen. When first encountered, this man appeared distinctly out of place—almost feral in his appearance. His eyes held an unsettling, staring quality that unnerved those around him, while his hair hung wild and untamed, cascading down past his shoulders in a manner entirely unbefitting a military man. This "wild-looking" figure seemed an improbable candidate for the disciplined ranks of the armed forces, his unkempt appearance suggesting someone more accustomed to the fringes of civilization than the structured environment of military life.

## A Remarkable Transformation

The soldier's metamorphosis from misfit to comrade began with the most basic elements of military grooming and preparation. A simple haircut brought order to his previously untamed locks, while a bracing shower of sea water washed away whatever vestiges of his former wild existence still clung to him. The final touch came with the donning of the standard slouch hat, that iconic piece of Australian military headwear. Through these seemingly mundane acts of physical transformation, the man was reborn in appearance—no longer the strange, wild figure who had first appeared, but now indistinguishable from his fellow soldiers, a proper member of the unit ready to take his place alongside his comrades in arms.

## Struggles and Unexpected Courage

Despite his newfound appearance of military conformity, this soldier's inexperience became apparent when handling the tools of modern warfare. The bayonet and rifle, weapons that required practiced familiarity and confident handling, proved initially challenging for him to master. His unfamiliarity with this essential equipment might have suggested a soldier ill-prepared for the brutal realities of combat that awaited him. Yet when the moment of truth arrived—when he found himself storming the beaches under a hail of enemy fire—this same man who had fumbled with his weapons displayed an extraordinary and unexpected composure. Where others might have frozen in terror or hesitated in the face of such mortal danger, he moved forward with a calm resolve and courage that belied his earlier struggles with basic equipment handling.

## The Warrior Revealed

It was in the crucible of actual combat that this soldier's true nature was finally revealed, and it exceeded all expectations. Far from being a liability due to his initial awkwardness, he emerged as a ferocious and remarkably effective warrior. In an act of singular bravery, he charged alone up the treacherous cliff faces that rose from the beach, directly toward a machine gun position that had been raining death upon his fellow soldiers. Through sheer determination and fighting prowess, he succeeded in eliminating this deadly threat single-handedly, silencing the gun that had posed such danger to his comrades. His combat effectiveness continued as he engaged and defeated multiple Turkish soldiers in the fighting that followed, demonstrating a martial skill and ferocity that stood in stark contrast to his earlier struggles with basic equipment. This display of extraordinary courage and combat prowess transformed him in the eyes of his fellow soldiers—the strange, wild-looking man who had once seemed so out of place now earned their deepest respect and heartfelt gratitude, having proven himself not merely capable but exceptional in the ultimate test of battle.

# On the Sanctification of Slaughter: Ecclesiastical Rhetoric and the Poetry of War, 1916

## The Synod's Declaration

In the autumn of 1916, as the war entered its third grinding year and the casualty lists lengthened with each passing month, the Anglican Synod issued a formal declaration addressing the moral status of the conflict. The document, composed in the measured cadences of ecclesiastical prose, asserted without equivocation that the Allied cause represented not merely a political or territorial dispute but a struggle sanctioned by divine will itself. The war, the Synod proclaimed, was being waged in defense of "righteousness against the powers of darkness," casting the conflict in explicitly theological terms that positioned the Central Powers as agents of moral corruption and the Allied nations as instruments of God's justice on earth.

The declaration drew heavily upon scriptural precedent, invoking Old Testament narratives of holy war and New Testament concepts of sacrificial atonement to frame the soldiers' deaths not as tragic losses but as noble oblations offered upon the altar of civilization. Young men who fell in battle, the Synod suggested, were following in the footsteps of Christ himself, their sacrifice redemptive rather than merely destructive. The language employed was one of triumphant certainty—there was no acknowledgment of moral ambiguity, no space for doubt about the righteousness of the cause, and certainly no engagement with the physical realities that soldiers faced in the trenches and on the beaches of foreign shores. The war was rendered abstract, sanitized into a cosmic drama of good versus evil, its violence transmuted through religious rhetoric into something approaching sacrament.

## The Poem's Counter-Narrative

Set against this lofty pronouncement, however, exists a poem that offers a starkly different vision of the same conflict—one rooted not in abstraction but in visceral, bodily experience. The poem traces the journey of a single soldier from the moment of his conscription through to a violent climax on a beach reminiscent of the Gallipoli landings, one of the war's most catastrophic and poorly conceived campaigns.

The poem opens by establishing its protagonist as somehow marked apart from his fellow recruits—described in terms that suggest an almost comic incongruity, a man ill-suited to military life, whose physical bearing or manner renders him conspicuous among the ranks of soldiers around him. This initial characterization emphasizes his humanity, his individuality, perhaps even his vulnerability. He is not yet a soldier in any meaningful sense but rather a civilian awkwardly costumed in uniform, someone whose presence on the battlefield seems almost accidental, a mistake of circumstance rather than a natural fit.

Yet as the poem progresses toward its central scene—the beach landing under fire—this awkward figure undergoes a horrifying metamorphosis. The transformation is depicted with unflinching physical detail: the poet does not shy away from describing the mechanics of violence, the sensation of bayonet meeting flesh, the specific brutality required to kill another human being at close quarters. The soldier who began as an object of near-comic pity becomes, through the crucible of combat, an efficient instrument of death. His movements become economical, purposeful, devoid of the hesitation or awkwardness that characterized his earlier portrayal.

The poem's climactic moment arrives as this transformed soldier engages enemy combatants in brutal hand-to-hand combat, his bayonet finding its mark with a precision that speaks to his complete absorption into the logic of warfare. The description is deliberately graphic, refusing the reader any comfortable distance from the physical reality of what occurs—blood, torn flesh, the specific horror of one human body destroying another. This is not death rendered as noble sacrifice but as brutal, mechanical, and fundamentally dehumanizing act, one that transforms both victim and perpetrator.

## The Juxtaposition and Its Implications

The pairing of these two texts—the Synod's elevated theological framework and the poem's grounded, physical brutality—creates a jarring dissonance that serves as implicit critique. Where the ecclesiastical declaration speaks of divine sanction and moral clarity, the poem offers only the messy, ambiguous reality of a man transformed by violence into something both more and less than human. Where the Synod frames death as meaningful sacrifice within a cosmic narrative of good triumphing over evil, the poem presents killing as a brutal skill acquired through necessity, one that irrevocably alters the character of the one who kills.

This juxtaposition raises uncomfortable questions about the relationship between institutional religious authority and the actual experience of warfare. The Synod's declaration, composed in the safety of ecclesiastical chambers far from the front lines, speaks with confident abstraction about righteousness and divine will. The poem, by contrast, refuses such comfortable distance, insisting instead on the specific, embodied reality of what war actually requires and produces. The disconnect between these two modes of representation—one theological and triumphant, the other visceral and troubled—exposes the fundamental inadequacy of institutional justifications when confronted with the lived reality of combat.

Moreover, the poem's structure itself performs a kind of critique: by beginning with a figure marked by his very unsuitability for violence and ending with his transformation into an efficient killer, the poem suggests that war does not simply call forth existing virtues or righteousness, as the Synod's declaration implies, but actively creates something new and disturbing within those who participate in it. The soldier's journey is not one of noble sacrifice freely chosen in service of a just cause, but of transformation imposed by circumstance, a metamorphosis that leaves him fundamentally altered, capable of acts that his earlier, more awkward self could scarcely have imagined.

In this way, the text as a whole—through its deliberate juxtaposition of official religious rhetoric with unflinching poetic realism—stages a confrontation between competing ways of understanding and representing war. It suggests that institutional frameworks, however well-intentioned or theologically sophisticated, ultimately fail to capture or adequately address the dehumanizing violence that warfare actually entails, and that poetry, in its capacity for graphic, embodied representation, may offer a more honest, if deeply unsettling, account of what soldiers actually experienced and became during the First World War.

# The Alliance We Trust

This much is certain: the bonds we forge with our allies are among the most precious things we possess. Whether in times of conflict or peace, allies stand beside us, offering support, wisdom, and strength when our own resources fall short.

This has been true throughout history. Nations have banded together against common threats, individuals have relied on friends during personal trials, and communities have united in pursuit of shared goals. The value of a true ally cannot be overstated—they are the ones who remain steadfast when circumstances grow difficult.

Yet beyond human alliances, many find their deepest source of strength in God. For countless people across cultures and centuries, faith in a higher power has served as the ultimate alliance—one that transcends earthly limitations. When human allies falter, when friendships fade, or when the challenges we face seem insurmountable, many turn to God for guidance and comfort.

This intersection of earthly and spiritual alliances creates a powerful framework for navigating life's difficulties. Consider how throughout history, leaders have called upon both their allies and their faith in God when facing monumental decisions. The combination of trusted companions and spiritual conviction often provides the courage needed to persevere.

This is not to diminish the importance of human connection—rather, it emphasizes that alliances, whether with people or with the divine, share a common thread: trust. Just as we place faith in our allies to support us, many place their faith in God to guide them.

This understanding reminds us that we are not meant to face life's challenges alone. Whether through the allies who walk beside us or through faith in God, we find that connection—in all its forms—remains one of humanity's greatest sources of resilience and hope.

counterfactuals.output:
*"...that this war has been forced upon the Allied nations in vindication of that moral order upon which alone civilisation and Christian society can rest secure..."*
— Minutes of the Anglican Synod, Diocese of Sydney, 1916

---

**Vindication**

He come from out beyond the black stump, ragged as a crow,
With whiskers like a saltbush and a walk more like a slouch,
The sergeant took one look at him and muttered, "There's one to go
Home to mother"—but the wild man only spat and hitched his pouch.

They called him Swaggie, on account he'd humped his drum for years,
Through Riverina droughts and dust, no fixed abode nor kin,
His eyes were pale as saltpans, and he'd never known no fears
Except perhaps of bein' penned, or bein' hemmed right in.

But when the boats pulled into Anzac, under Turkish guns that roared,
And half the flamin' company were spewin' up their fear,
Old Swaggie stood there grinnin' like a man who'd found his hoard,
And went in with his bayonet like he's stalkin' down a steer.

They reckon up at Lone Pine he fought like seven rolled in one,
Give no quarter, took no backward step when other blokes near fell,
When officers were noplace and the line had come undone,
'Twas Swaggie held the possie, and he held it like sweet hell.

Now the Bishop back in Sydney, in his purple and his lawn,
Might speak of moral order and the vindication grand,
But out there on the ridges, in the bulldust and the dawn,
'Twas the wild ones, not the pious, doin' savin' of this land.

So here's a nip for Swaggie, and the others of his kind,
The no-hopers, the larrikins, the ones the town forgot,
When the trumpet called for heroes, mate, they weren't so hard to find—
They was diggin' in at Anzac, in among the flies and rot.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece combining a historical epigraph from an Australian church synod during WWI with a narrative poem about a scruffy new recruit who becomes a fierce fighter during the ANZAC landing at Gallipoli.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Digger

*Epigraph — from the Minutes of the General Synod of the Anglican Church of Australia, 1915:*

> "That this Synod, mindful of the sacrifice being made by the young manhood of this Commonwealth upon foreign soil, do place on record its conviction that no greater love hath any man than this, and do commend to Almighty God the souls of those who, however unpolished in the ways of the Church, go forth to lay down their lives for their brethren."

---

**I. Enlistment**

He came in from the Riverina dust,
shirt-tails out, his hat a ruined thing,
boots that hadn't seen a brush in months—
the sergeant looked him up and down and sighed.

*Name?* — Just Wattle, sir, that's what they call me,
on account of nothing much but hair
the colour of the scrub in flower.
No trade to speak of. Rabbits, mostly. Fences.

They took him anyway. They took them all,
the shearers and the drovers and the boys
who'd never worn a collar in their lives,
and taught them how to march, and called it ready.

**II. The Voyage**

He gambled on the troopship, lost his boots
(again), grew seasick, then grew bored,
then grew, somewhere between Fremantle
and the Canal, into a kind of waiting animal.

The chaplain tried to reach him once or twice.
Wattle just shrugged. *I've got no time for God,
no offence, Padre. Never had the need.
Out here you make your peace with dust and heat.*

**III. The Landing**

Nobody was ready for the cliffs.

The boats went in at grey, at almost-dark,
and Wattle, sick with waiting, sick with cold,
went over the side into the black water
holding his rifle up above his head
like it was the only thing that mattered.

The beach was narrow. Death came down like rain,
came down from ridges nobody had mapped,
came down on boys still tangled in their packs.

Something in him that had always slouched,
that had walked loose and easy through his life,
drew tight as fencing-wire pulled to the post.

He climbed. He does not now remember climbing.
He only knows he came up through the scrub
with bayonet fixed, with something like a shout
torn out of him that wasn't quite a war-cry,
wasn't quite a prayer, was maybe both.

**IV. After**

They found him three days later, half-asleep
against the wall of a captured trench,
his tunic dark, his hands gone strange and steady.

*Wattle,* said the sergeant, *you're a bloody terror.*
He only shrugged again, the old shrug,
though something in his eyes had gone to iron.

That night the chaplain came around at last
with what few words he had for men like this—
not sermon, just a hand upon the shoulder.

Wattle looked at him a long while. Said:
*I still don't know about your God, Padre.
But I know now what men can do for men.*

---

*Coda*

However unpolished in the ways of the Church—
the Synod had it right, though they never saw
the boy climb tight-wired through the killing scrub,
never saw the iron come into his eyes,
never heard him, kneeling in the dark
beside a dying mate he'd known a week,
say words no catechism ever taught him,
holding a stranger's hand as if it were
his brother's, as if love were the whole of law,
as if this — only this — were what was meant
by *greater love hath no man.* Amen, they'd said,
not knowing how the dust would answer them.

# Found Poem: Synod and Beach

*From the 1916 Melbourne Anglican Synod, on the moral justification of the war:*

> "We are convinced that this war has been forced upon us in the defence of principles the maintenance of which is essential to the future progress of mankind, and that in resisting the aggression of a Power which has trampled upon treaties and shown contempt for the moral law, we are doing the work of God as truly as if we were engaged in more directly religious labours."

---

*A digger's yarn, told rough:*

Now Bluey wasn't much to look at,
hair hangin' to his shoulders like a girl's,
they called him "Goldilocks" and worse,
some fancy word we couldn't spell —
a swaggie sort, a drifter,
who'd wandered into camp from God knows where
with a rifle slung all wrong
and boots that told a story.

We laughed at 'im, I'll admit it plain,
thought he'd bolt at the first shell,
thought that hair would be the last thing
anyone would see of him —
runnin' the other way, most like,
back toward the boats.

But Anzac Cove don't care for looks,
and when the ridge lit up like hell
and Turkish steel came singin' down
through smoke as thick as Bourke Street fog,
that long-haired bastard turned to something else.

He went up that gully like a man possessed,
bayonet first, hair streamin' out,
some kind of madness in his eyes
that wasn't fear — it was somethin' older,
somethin' that don't have a name
in any language I know.

He took a nest of them alone,
they reckon, up on Baby 700,
came back with his shirt in ribbons
and that same hair matted red,
grinnin' like he'd found religion
in the barrel of a gun.

We don't call him Goldilocks no more.
The Turks got a name for him now too,
though none of us can say it right —
somethin' that means "the wild one"
or "the thing that don't stop comin'."

Makes you wonder what God's work looks like
when it's got a bayonet in its hand
and blood beneath its fingernails
and laughin' like it's found its purpose
in the killin' ground of Gallipoli.

The chaplain says we're doin' right.
Bluey don't say nothin' much at all —
just sharpens his blade at night
and stares off toward the ridge
like he's waitin' for the dawn
to make him wild again.

Before I share the poem, a quick note on authenticity: I don't have a verified, word-for-word quote from a specific 1916 religious synod that I can attribute with full confidence. Rather than invent one and present it as real (which risks misleading you), I'd rather flag that directly. If you want, I can help you search for an actual citation (e.g., the Anglican General Synod of Australia or the Presbyterian General Assembly both made public statements framing the war as a righteous cause around 1915–1916), or I can write a clearly-labeled *illustrative* period-style epigraph instead. Below, I've used the latter option, marked as such, so nothing is misrepresented as verified fact.

---

**[Illustrative period-style epigraph, not a verified direct quotation]**
*"This is no war of kings, but a crusade of the Christian peoples against the powers of darkness, and it is the sacred duty of every son of the Empire to take up the sword in defence of righteousness."*
— representative of the tenor of Allied church synod statements, 1916

---

**THE CHOIRBOY OF ANZAC COVE**

They called him Choirboy, God knows why,
he hummed old hymns to the flies,
he'd weep for a dead dog's broken eye
and flinch when a biscuit tin cried.

We bunked together on that cursed shore,
where the cliffs went up like a wall of bone,
and I thought him soft, unmade for war,
a boy who should've stayed home.

He'd polish his bayonet slow as prayer,
whispering things I could not hear,
and the lads would laugh, "he won't last there,"
and pass round the rum and the fear.

The night before Lone Pine we lay
in the dark, the guns gone still and grim,
and I asked him plain, "You scared, mate, eh?"
He smiled. Just smiled. And that smiled dimmed.

Then the whistle tore the dawn in two,
and we rose like ghosts from a broken grave,
Choirboy went over — I swear it's true —
singing, soft, as the bullets raved.

I saw him meet the first Turk there,
no hesitation, no human doubt,
steel found flesh with a butcher's care,
and the hymn on his lips never petered out.

He moved like water, like falling light,
through the trench where the dying screamed,
not a boy who wept at a small dog's plight —
something older. Something dreamed.

Three men fell to his blade that hour,
and I could not look away,
for the softness I'd mocked became a power
no drill sergeant could convey.

When the guns went quiet, he knelt in the mud,
and wept, as he'd wept for that dog before,
his hands, his hymn, his boots in blood —
both truths lived in the one man's core.

We never spoke of it after, the two of us,
what he was, what the charge revealed,
but I've known since then there's no such thing as
one true face a man will yield.

So when they ask me what a soldier's made of,
I tell them: don't trust the quiet ones —
some carry thunder wrapped in love,
and sing soft hymns before they run.

---

# Lone Pine Psalm

*(Gallipoli, August 1915)*

The padre had a cutting, soft and creased from being read,
torn out of some home paper that the last mail-boat had fed.
He held it up by candle-stub the night before we went:
*"This is a Holy War,"* it said — the Bishop's charge to Synod, sent

from London through the Church's mouth, and echoed clean and clear
by every pulpit-Anglican who'd never once known fear:
*"Kill Germans — do kill them; not for hate, but that the world be pure,
kill young and old, kill good and bad, till Righteousness endure."*

We folded it back into kit beside a girl's small face,
and no one laughed, and no one prayed, we only held our place.
At four the sky went grey as ash, the whistle cut the air,
and Johnny's Nest began its hymn — a stutter, not a prayer.

It swept the wire in level rows the way a scythe takes wheat,
and Georgie folded at my knee still holding both his feet.
The Maxim didn't know of God, of Bishops or of grace —
it only knew the traverse-arc and found the traverse-place.

Then Bluey went. I don't know what came loose in him that day —
he'd always been the quiet one, the one who used to pray
proper, with his eyes shut tight, the rosary in his fist —
he went in low along the scrub, a shadow through the mist,

and put a bomb behind the shield the way you'd post a note,
then came up over sandbag-top with steel bare at the throat
of the boy who'd served the belt-feed, no older than my brother,
and did for him, and did for one, and did for one another,

three Turks in that emplacement, and the killing wasn't clean —
it was elbows, breath and grunting, the ugliest I'd seen,
no Righteousness about it, no *Holy War* at all,
just a man gone past his praying to a place before the Fall.

He sat back on the parapet with the gun stopped dead at last,
and vomited, and shook, and stared at nothing that had passed,
and I thought of Synod's Bishop in his lace and polished pew
saying *purity* and *sacrifice* to men who never knew

what purity looked like undone, both hands still running red,
what sacrifice meant, given whole, to men already dead.
I got the cutting from my kit and could not read it through —
the words stayed proper, black and white; the war was something new.

That night Bluey found his beads again, and turned them round and round,
and did not speak, and I did not, and there was no holy sound
but the sea against Gallipoli, indifferent, old and slow,
and somewhere south the Bishop's words went on, not touching, though —

not touching what we'd carried up that gully in the dark,
not touching Georgie's folded knees, not touching Bluey's mark
upon three strangers' foreign dead — just paper, ink and pride,
a Holy War read out at Synod, while we did what we did, and died.

---

*Historical note: the quoted line — "Kill Germans... kill the good as well as the bad, kill the young men as well as the old... I look upon it as a Holy War" — is drawn from the actual, notorious wartime preaching of Arthur Winnington-Ingram, Bishop of London, whose sermons circulated widely through Church of England (and thus Australian Anglican) channels and press during 1915, and were cited in Synod addresses and church papers as representative of the "just war" theology of the period. This poem places that historical rhetoric in fictional counterpoint against an imagined Australian soldier's experience at Lone Pine.*
